Shamwari Vultures

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A lifeline for some of Southern Africa's most endangered vultures...

Unique Selling Point:
it's the largest relocation of vultures ever undertaken. 155 White-backed and Cape vultures are being moved from Vulpro at Hartebeespoort to Shamwari in the Eastern Cape. And the new facility will be officially opened on 23 January 2024.

Summary:
Vulpro is synonymous with vulture conservation. For over a decade they have been breeding and rehabilitating vultures, releasing these birds to supplement dwindling populations in the wild. And their space in Hartbeespoort has become too small for the important work they are doing. So, they are moving to a new bespoke facility in the Eastern Cape and will enjoy the unspoilt wilderness at Shamwari Private Game Reserve.

VulPro is able to save many vultures that would otherwise have met their untimely deaths. By doing this, VulPro is in a position to release the vultures that are fit and healthy and to keep those that cannot be released in captivity for breeding, research, and educational purposes. Vulture populations are, in many instances, so depleted that the rehabilitation and release of individual birds can be ecologically and genetically significant.

Further information:
Non-releasable vultures that come into VulPro for rehabilitation form part of the ex-situ population and are bred to produce individuals which form part of our pilot release studies. GPS transmitters are placed on all released individuals and this data then forms part of our research programmes. We incorporate population monitoring through maintaining a re-sighting database utilising camera traps, photographs and recordings from the general public and, monitoring wild vulture breeding sites. Our presence in the field following vultures has increased landowner engagement as well as improved vulture awareness and this information assists us to keep up to date with anthropomorphic changes in the vulture’s environment which, enables us to keep up with threats and appropriate mitigation measures within different areas. All information gained feeds into our investigative research and often leads to full blown research projects.

Flights to PE (And Back)
Accommodation - 3 people 1 night

Script:


SHAMWARI VULTURES


This is Percy – a Cape Vulture… – a threatened species with only around 10,000 individuals left in the wild…

As he sits here, perched in his new home in the Eastern Cape, he seems blissfully unaware of the vital role he has played in the conservation of African vultures….


Having a vulture chick in your hand you understand the fragility of the species.


Over two decades ago, baby Percy sparked an idea for what would become the largest Vulture conservation NGO on the African Continent…

And, in a round-about way, he’s the reason I find myself in the Eastern Cape, about to witness history in the making…



BREAK


I’m on my way to Shamwari Private Game Reserve, with one of my regular road trip companions – camerawoman, Alti…

Known internationally for its 5-star hospitality, the reserve is home to the Big 5…


Ag, a little skilpadjie is in the road…. A tortoise…. Let’s try and save it and get off the road…

Cheers… enjoy your tortoise life…


We’ve been invited to the unveiling of a new project here, in collaboration with Vulture conservation NGO, Vulpro.


Jéan: Afternoon, Mac. Mind your head. Have a seat.

Jéan: Welcome aboard.


Jéan Taute is Assistant Safari Operations Manager – and our guide for the next two days…
Interaction

Jéan: Okay, so my rifle in front of you here, please do not touch. This one's for you, alright?

Mac: This is all I get? You get a rifle, I get a stick!

Jéan: That’s the “Stick of truth”, that one.


Jéan: Are you ready to go?

Mac: I’m good.

Jéan: Perfect, let’s make our way…




This is 25,000 hectares of privately owned land with an impressive conservation history…


Jéan: The reserve was established in 1992, so we’re now heading into our thirty second year.

Mac: 32 Years! Oh okay.

Jéan: Proud to say we’re the first private game reserve in the Eastern Cape and going from strength to strength. I mean, here you are for another magnificent project kicking off, and there’s constantly new stuff happening.



It’s a fairly cool day for this time of the year, and the veld is teeming with herbivores enjoying the lush vegetation after some much-needed recent rain.


Jéan: That Springbok looked a little bit alert earlier… Alti! Jy’s braaf nê…


While Alti does a quick equipment check, Jéan keeps a lookout for whatever might have spooked the springbok…


Mac: You think they might be hunted?

Jéan: Ja.


In the distance a warthog family makes a run for it … – Clearly something is lurking in the tall grass…


Jéan: There!

Mac: What Lion?

Jéan: Nope. Something different…


We head towards a slight koppie in the distance…


Mac: There they are! There they are!

Jéan: Good job.


Two beautiful cheetahs –, surveying the landscape.


Mac: Wow!

Jéan: How cool is that?

Mac: Oh man!...


While this is starting to feel very much like a holiday safari, we didn’t come for the cheetahs… – we’re here for Percy and his friends…
LINK
These guys know the secrets of what happens out in nature…. Who took out who, who killed who… because after every kill they come in and clean up…


These are critically endangered white-backed vultures, endemic to sub-saharan Africa.
Once common and widespread, their numbers have declined by over 90% since the 1980’s...

But these specific birds are key to slowing the slide towards possible extinction.
Kerri
This is the first phase of a 2-year project…


Kerri Wolter is the founder and CEO of Vulpro.
Kerri
Here we go… This is my boy.

Mac: Is this Percy?

This is him….


Kerri’s journey in vulture conservation started 21 years ago, with Percy.
Kerri
I had him from 10 days old and he did extensive education and awareness work with me until he decided he had enough.

Mac: Do you guys have a bit of a relationship, though?

Yes, but I still won’t touch him. When he bites, he bites.


Vulpro was established in 2007 and focuses on vulture rehabilitation, as well as captive breeding & reintroduction programmes.
Kerri
Vultures can withstand anything, pretty much, thrown at them from a natural point of view. From diseases, from viruses, from anything… What they can’t withstand is when man comes into play.
Kerri
We cannot anymore just protect vultures in their natural habitat. We need to do more because of the rate of decline…


After almost 2 decades, it was time for Vulpro to spread its wings, as it were…


But moving 163 white-backed and Cape vultures across the country was no easy task.
Katja
Mac: When they came to and said that they wanted to relocate 163 birds from Hearties all the way to the Eastern Cape. Your heart must have skipped a beat, right?

Katja: More than one. We actually didn't start at 163. We started at 140. And then Kerri kept adding one or two. And eventually I got there and they’re like, oh it’s 162. And then I found an extra one and there was 163.


Prof. Katja Koeppel from the University of Pretoria was in charge of the birds’ welfare… – because even though vultures are naturally accustomed to travelling great distances, this trip was very different…
Katja
We had less than 2 minutes apart between catching, putting it in the box and onto the truck.


The entire operation took about 18 hours, and is said to be the largest vulture relocation ever undertaken…
Katja
There was a lot of logistics. And then, you know, how many boxes do you fit? What's the dimension of the box? How do we put it onto the truck? And then we needed to have ventilation going…
Johan
We had to make sure that the birds wouldn’t overheat and start stressing because on a long trip that’s not ideal.


Shamwari Veterinarian, Dr Johan Joubert, was hands-on during the process.
Johan
We always think; medical treatment, but in wildlife prevention is much more important than anything. And we must anticipate problems and prevent that.


Once the trucks were loaded, they set off on a nerve-wracking 1000-kilometre journey…
Katja
Every 2 to 3 hours we stopped and we checked the birds. We looked through the holes with torches. We checked that they were okay, that nobody was getting too cold, too hot. Everybody was settled.


The trucks with their precious cargo arrived at Shamwari around noon on the 22nd of January…
Johan
Yesterday when we started releasing those birds, that was extremely special and an emotional moment for us…


This new Vulpro facility consists of 4 large enclosures, to cater to the specific needs of each group.


These are the Cape Vulture breeders that should start producing eggs by April.

Since there are virtually no wild Cape Vultures left here in the Eastern Cape, it’s up to Percy and his friends to produce a new generation, and new hope…
Johan
You know birds that get extinct in a specific area, and we bring them back, it’s very special. Personally I didn’t like the idea of animals in Captivity or birds in captivity, but this is different because the offspring are going to re-populate the area.


For Shamwari CEO, Joe Cloete, this collaboration is a no-brainer…
Joe Cloete
Bringing 163 vultures back to Shamwari, or back to the Eastern Cape, you know, is as important as 163 black rhino or 163 wild dog. It’s just part of the greater conservation journey that we’ve embarked on for the last 32 years.
Kerri
Mac: So Kerri, how did you get to Shamwari, why specifically Shamwari?

Kerri: As a non-Profit organisation you look at partnering with an organisation that has a very good reputation, but that is stable, secure now and into the future. You know, because what we don’t want to do is relocate and in a year or two year’s time there’s insecurities.


With our time at Shamwari coming to an end, Jéan has one last surprise in store…


Jean
Here we have the pre-release camp, which is going to be the birds first to set wings and be able to call the skies above Shamwari their new home… So, if you want to hop out…


We are careful to not disturb these birds. They have been successfully rehabilitated, and should have as little human contact as possible.

Very soon they will fly again…
Jean
Of course one of the important things they need, is height… So up here it’s perfectly situated because there’s good wind up here…
And then the next important thing is… if you look over there in the distance there’s a beautiful cliff which ideally – if all goes according to plan – These Cape Vultures are going to settle on there, and they’re going to start breeding in the area …


Who knows… – in the not-so-distant future, one of Percy’s offspring may just decide,
to call this home…














PROMO 1 21”
In an unprecedented operation, 163 vultures were moved across the country to help secure a future for some of our most vulnerable and endangered birds.

UPS Katja Koeppel
It was months of planning…
We had less than 2 minutes a bird; between catching, putting it in the box and onto the truck.




PROMO 2 21”
An encounter that sparked almost 2 decades in vulture conservation.

Having a vulture chick in your hand you understand the fragility of the species.

Now, a groundbreaking partnership between Vulpro and Shamwari Private Game Reserve is hoping to secure the future of African Vultures.




PROMO 3 21”
Over the last 30 years their numbers have plummeted…

We cannot anymore just protect vultures in their natural habitat. We need to do more because of the rate of decline…

In a first-of-its-kind relocation operation, conservationists take a bold step towards protecting some of our most threatened vulture species…

VulPro is able to save many vultures that would otherwise have met their untimely deaths. By doing this, VulPro is in a position to release the vultures that are fit and healthy and to keep those that cannot be released in captivity for breeding, research, and educational purposes. Vulture populations are, in many instances, so depleted that the rehabilitation and release of individual birds can be ecologically and genetically significant.
metadata.Further information: Non-releasable vultures that come into VulPro for rehabilitation form part of the ex-situ population and are bred to produce individuals which form part of our pilot release studies. GPS transmitters are placed on all released individuals and this data then forms part of our research programmes. We incorporate population monitoring through maintaining a re-sighting database utilising camera traps, photographs and recordings from the general public and, monitoring wild vulture breeding sites. Our presence in the field following vultures has increased landowner engagement as well as improved vulture awareness and this information assists us to keep up to date with anthropomorphic changes in the vulture’s environment which, enables us to keep up with threats and appropriate mitigation measures within different areas. All information gained feeds into our investigative research and often leads to full blown research projects.
